rules.reference: N.K. Chauhan v. State of Gujarat
rules.relevance: Held that seniority is normally measured by the length of continuous officiating service and that quota is not so interlocked with rota that the latter is impliedly inscribed.

rules.case_name: S.B. Patwardhan v. State of Maharashtra
rules.reference: S.B. Patwardhan v. State of Maharashtra
rules.relevance: Held that continuous officiation in a non-fortuitous vacancy ought to receive due recognition in determining seniority.

rules.case_name: Ajit Singh II v. State of Punjab
rules.reference: Ajit Singh II v. State of Punjab
rules.relevance: Established that roster point promotions do not confer seniority over general candidates who reach the same level through normal promotion channels; seniority must be determined by normal rules.

rules.case_name: Direct Recruit Class II Engineering Officers' Association v. State of Maharashtra
rules.reference: Direct Recruit Class II Engineering Officers' Association v. State of Maharashtra
rules.relevance: Laid down that ad hoc appointments not made according to rules (stop-gap arrangements) cannot count for seniority unless regularized in accordance with rules.

rules.case_name: Bishan Swaroop Gupta v. Union of India
rules.reference: Bishan Swaroop Gupta v. Union of India (1st Bishan Swaroop Gupta case)
rules.relevance: The court relied on this case for the principle that if the quota rule collapses or is not strictly observed, the linked seniority rule also ceases to be operative, and for the definition of permanent vs. fortuitous vacancies.

rules.case_name: V. S. Badami v. State of Mysore
rules.reference: V. S. Badami v. State of Mysore
rules.relevance: The court relied on this case for the principle that promotions made in excess of quota are irregular and promotees cannot claim rights unless vacancies fall within their quota.

rules.reference: Seniority based on length of continuous officiation
rules.relevance: The court held that in the absence of a specific statutory rule, seniority must be determined on the basis of length of continuous officiation in the grade.

rules.reference: Invalidity of rotational seniority with massive quota deviation
rules.relevance: The court held that applying a rotational rule of seniority when there is massive and continuous deviation from the quota rule results in gross discrimination and is unconstitutional.

rules.case_name: Sural Prakash Gupta v. State of J&K
rules.reference: Sural Prakash Gupta v. State of J&K
rules.relevance: Held that ad hoc service could count for seniority if specific rules permitted retrospective regularization; distinguished here as no such rule exists in Nagaland.

rules.reference: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016
rules.relevance: Prescribes the 30-day limitation period for filing appeals to the NCLAT, with a proviso allowing condonation of delay up to 15 days if sufficient cause is shown, creating an outer limit of 45 days.

rules.reference: National Company Law Appellate Tribunal Rules, 2016
rules.relevance: Mandates that every appeal shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the impugned order, which is central to the dispute over the free copy provided by the Registry.

rules.reference: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016
rules.relevance: Provides that the provisions of the Limitation Act, 1963, apply as far as may be to proceedings and appeals before the NCLAT, which is relevant to the condonation of delay.

rules.reference: Limitation Act, 1963
rules.relevance: Mandates that the day from which the period of limitation is to be reckoned (the date of pronouncement) shall be excluded, which is relevant to calculating the delay.

rules.reference: Limitation Act, 1963
rules.relevance: Requires the exclusion of the time requisite for obtaining a copy of the order appealed from, provided the application for the copy was made within the prescribed limitation period, which is central to the dispute over the free copy.

rules.case_name: V Nagarajan v. SKS Ispat and Power Limited & Ors
rules.reference: V Nagarajan v. SKS Ispat and Power Limited & Ors
rules.relevance: Established that limitation commences upon pronouncement and time for obtaining a certified copy is excluded only if an application is made within the limitation period, which is directly relevant to the facts of this case.

rules.reference: Limitation Act, 1963
rules.relevance: Allows condonation of delay if sufficient cause is shown, which is directly relevant to the appellant's application for condonation of delay.

rules.reference: Limitation Act, 1963
rules.relevance: Excludes time requisite for obtaining a certified copy from limitation computation, but the Explanation clarifies that time taken by the court to prepare the order before an application is made is not excluded. Thus, an application must be filed to trigger the exclusion, which is central to the dispute over the free copy.

rules.case_name: Sagufa Ahmed v. Upper Assam Plywood Products Pvt Ltd
rules.reference: Sagufa Ahmed v. Upper Assam Plywood Products Pvt Ltd
rules.relevance: Held that under the Companies Act, limitation runs from when the copy is made available. The court distinguished this, noting the IBC is a special code with stricter timelines and different statutory language, which is relevant to the dispute over the free copy.

rules.case_name: Mobilox Innovations Private Ltd v. Kirusa Software Private Ltd
rules.reference: Mobilox Innovations Private Ltd v. Kirusa Software Private Ltd
rules.relevance: Emphasized that timelines are sacrosanct under the IBC to ensure time-bound resolution and prevent protracted proceedings, which is relevant to the strict adherence to limitation periods in this case.

rules.reference: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908
rules.relevance: Mandates that a second appeal lies only if it involves a substantial question of law. Sub-section (4) imposes a duty on the High Court to formulate such questions. Sub-section (5) requires the appeal to be heard on the formulated questions, ensuring parties can argue on them.

rules.case_name: Ishwar Dass Jain v. Sohan Lal
rules.reference: Ishwar Dass Jain v. Sohan Lal
rules.relevance: Established that it is essential for the High Court to formulate a substantial question of law and it is not permissible to reverse the judgment of the first appellate court without doing so.

rules.case_name: Roop Singh v. Ram Singh
rules.reference: Roop Singh v. Ram Singh
rules.relevance: Confirmed that the jurisdiction of the High Court under Section 100 is confined to appeals involving a substantial question of law and does not extend to interfering with pure questions of fact.

rules.case_name: Kanhaiyalal & Ors. Versus Anupkumar & Ors.
rules.reference: Kanhaiyalal & Ors. Versus Anupkumar & Ors.
rules.relevance: Established that the High Court must satisfy itself that a substantial question of law is involved before entertaining a second appeal and must formulate it.

rules.case_name: Chadat Singh Versus Bahadur Ram & Ors.
rules.reference: Chadat Singh Versus Bahadur Ram & Ors.
rules.relevance: Reinforced the mandatory nature of formulating a substantial question of law under Section 100 CPC.

rules.case_name: Sasikumar & Ors. Versus Kunnath Chellappan Nair & Others
rules.reference: Sasikumar & Ors. Versus Kunnath Chellappan Nair & Others
rules.relevance: Cited to support the proposition that the High Court must formulate the substantial question of law.

rules.case_name: Joseph Severance & Ors. Versus Benny Mathew & Ors.
rules.reference: Joseph Severance & Ors. Versus Benny Mathew & Ors.
rules.relevance: Cited to support the proposition that the High Court must formulate the substantial question of law.

rules.reference: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908
rules.relevance: The court relied on this provision to establish that a second appeal must be heard only on the substantial questions of law framed by the High Court under Section 100(4).

rules.case_name: Surat Singh (Dead) vs. Siri Bhagwan & Ors.
rules.reference: Surat Singh (Dead) vs. Siri Bhagwan & Ors.
rules.relevance: Cited to support the principle that the High Court's power to hear an appeal on additional substantial questions of law under the proviso to Section 100(5) is exercisable only after assigning reasons for framing such additional questions.

rules.case_name: Hardeep Kaur vs. Malkiat Kaur
rules.reference: Hardeep Kaur vs. Malkiat Kaur
rules.relevance: Reiterated that the formulation of a substantial question of law is a sine qua non for the exercise of jurisdiction under Section 100 CPC.

rules.reference: Industrial Disputes Act, 1947
rules.relevance: Defines 'workman' to include persons employed for clerical work for hire or reward, regardless of whether the employment is regular, temporary, or contractual. Relevant to determining if the appellant qualifies as a 'workman' despite supervisory role.

rules.reference: Industrial Disputes Act, 1947
rules.relevance: Imposes mandatory conditions precedent to retrenchment, including one month's notice (or pay in lieu) and retrenchment compensation for workmen with continuous service of one year or more. Relevant to assessing compliance with termination procedures.

rules.case_name: U.P. State Brassware Corporation Ltd. & another vs. Uday Narain Pandey
rules.reference: U.P. State Brassware Corporation Ltd. & another vs. Uday Narain Pandey
rules.relevance: Established that reinstatement with back wages is not automatic for illegal termination and that compensation is a discretionary alternative. Relevant to the Labour Court's decision on reinstatement.

rules.case_name: Haryana State Electronics Development Corporation vs. Mamni
rules.reference: Haryana State Electronics Development Corporation vs. Mamni
rules.relevance: Supported the view that the legal position has shifted away from mandatory reinstatement with back wages. Relevant to the High Court's decision to set aside reinstatement.

rules.reference: Discretionary nature of relief in illegal termination cases
rules.relevance: Labour Courts have discretion to award compensation instead of reinstatement, considering factors like delay and prior payments. Relevant to the Labour Court's decision to award compensation instead of reinstatement.

rules.case_name: Anoop Sharma v. Executive Engineer, Public Health Division, Haryana
rules.reference: Anoop Sharma v. Executive Engineer, Public Health Division, Haryana
rules.relevance: Held that termination without complying with mandatory provisions of Section 25-F should ordinarily result in reinstatement. Relevant to the Labour Court's decision on reinstatement.

rules.case_name: State Bank of India v. N. Sundara Money
rules.reference: State Bank of India v. N. Sundara Money
rules.relevance: Established that 'retrenchment' has an expansive definition and that violation of Section 25-F renders termination null and void. Relevant to assessing the legality of the termination.

rules.case_name: Assistant Engineer, Rajasthan Development Corporation and Anr. v. Gitam Singh
rules.reference: Assistant Engineer, Rajasthan Development Corporation and Anr. v. Gitam Singh
rules.relevance: Reiterated that Labour Courts must consider mode of appointment, nature of employment, length of service, and delay in raising dispute before granting relief. Relevant to the Labour Court's decision on reinstatement.

rules.reference: Compensation in lieu of reinstatement
rules.relevance: The court applied the principle that in cases of long-drawn litigation and small length of service, compensation may be awarded instead of reinstatement to meet the interest of justice. Relevant to the High Court's decision to set aside reinstatement.

rules.case_name: General Manager, Haryana Roadways Vs. Rudhan Singh
rules.reference: General Manager, Haryana Roadways Vs. Rudhan Singh
rules.relevance: The court relied on this precedent for the principle that reinstatement with full back-wages is not automatic and depends on factors like length of service and nature of appointment. Relevant to the Labour Court's decision on reinstatement.

rules.reference: Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973
rules.relevance: Relevant to the High Court's decision to direct further investigation, as Section 311 empowers the court to summon material witnesses or recall/re-examine persons at any stage of the trial if their evidence is essential to the arrival of a just decision.

rules.reference: Code of Criminal Procedure (Cr.PC)
rules.relevance: Directly addresses the issue of further investigation at the post-cognizance stage, which was the basis for the High Court's order directing further investigation.

rules.case_name: Hardeep Singh and Ors. Vs. State of Punjab & Ors.
rules.reference: Hardeep Singh and Ors. Vs. State of Punjab & Ors.
rules.relevance: Establishes the standard for exercising power under Section 319 Cr.P.C., requiring strong and cogent evidence more than a prima facie case but short of satisfaction that unrebutted evidence would lead to conviction, which is relevant to the High Court's decision.

rules.case_name: Sagar vs. State of U.P. and Anr.
rules.reference: Sagar vs. State of U.P. and Anr.
rules.relevance: Reinforces the caution that the power under Section 319 should be exercised sparingly and only when circumstances warrant, applying the test laid down in Hardeep Singh, which is relevant to the High Court's decision.

rules.reference: Standard for exercising power under Section 319 Cr.P.C.
rules.relevance: Applies the principle that summoning an additional accused requires evidence that is more than prima facie but short of satisfaction that unrebutted evidence would lead to conviction, and cannot be based on mere suspicion, which is relevant to the High Court's decision.

rules.reference: Appellate court's duty to appreciate evidence rather than remand
rules.relevance: Holds that the High Court should have appreciated the material on record to decide on summoning rather than remanding the matter, to avoid prolonging litigation, which is relevant to the High Court's decision.

rules.case_name: Michael Machado and Anr. v. Central Bureau of Investigation and Anr.
rules.reference: Michael Machado and Anr. v. Central Bureau of Investigation and Anr.
rules.relevance: Established that the power under Section 319 is discretionary, requires reasonable satisfaction from evidence, and must be exercised judicially considering the stage of trial and quantum of evidence to achieve criminal justice, which is relevant to the High Court's decision.

rules.case_name: Krishnappa v. State of Karnataka
rules.reference: Krishnappa v. State of Karnataka
rules.relevance: Emphasized that the power to summon an accused is extraordinary, should be used sparingly, and requires compelling reasons beyond mere mechanical addition based on some evidence, which is relevant to the High Court's decision.

rules.reference: Evidence vs. Materials
rules.relevance: Holds that Section 319 can only be exercised based on evidence adduced in court (witness testimony), not on materials available in the charge-sheet or case diary which do not constitute evidence, which is relevant to the High Court's decision.

rules.case_name: Rajesh v. State of Haryana
rules.reference: Rajesh v. State of Haryana
rules.relevance: Establishes that failure to file a protest petition does not preclude the court from exercising powers under Section 319 CrPC, which is relevant to the High Court's decision.

rules.reference: Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967
rules.relevance: This provision mandates that bail shall not be granted if the Court is of the opinion that there are reasonable grounds for believing that the accusation against the accused is prima facie true, which is relevant to the Appellant's bail application.

rules.reference: Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967
rules.relevance: This section punishes conspiracy, attempt, or acts preparatory to the commission of a terrorist act, which is relevant to the Appellant's alleged participation in meetings and protests.

rules.case_name: National Investigation Agency vs. Zahoor Ahmad Shah Watali
rules.reference: National Investigation Agency vs. Zahoor Ahmad Shah Watali
rules.relevance: This judgment establishes that 'prima facie true' requires a finding based on broad probabilities, without elaborate examination or dissection of evidence, and that admissibility of evidence is not a ground to discard material at the bail stage, which is relevant to the Appellant's arguments regarding the seizure of documents.

rules.case_name: Gurwinder Singh vs. State of Punjab and Another
rules.reference: Gurwinder Singh vs. State of Punjab and Another
rules.relevance: This decision summarizes the guidelines from Watali's case regarding the application of Section 43D(5) UAPA, which is relevant to the Appellant's bail application.

rules.reference: Constitution of India
rules.relevance: This provision holds that the right to life and liberty includes access to justice and a speedy trial, justifying bail when trial is delayed, which is relevant to the Appellant's prolonged custody.

rules.case_name: Shaheen Welfare Association v. Union of India
rules.reference: Shaheen Welfare Association v. Union of India
rules.relevance: This case relies on the principle that gross delay in disposal of cases justifies invocation of Article 21 and release of undertrials on bail, which is relevant to the Appellant's prolonged custody.

rules.case_name: Hussain v. Union of India
rules.reference: Hussain v. Union of India
rules.relevance: This case supports the argument that protracted incarceration violates the right to speedy trial and access to justice, which is relevant to the Appellant's prolonged custody.

rules.case_name: Supreme Court Legal Aid Committee Representing Undertrial Prisoners v. Union of India
rules.reference: Supreme Court Legal Aid Committee Representing Undertrial Prisoners v. Union of India
rules.relevance: This case relies on the principle that undertrials cannot be indefinitely detained pending trial, which is relevant to the Appellant's prolonged custody.

rules.case_name: Union of India v. K.A. Najeeb
rules.reference: Union of India v. K.A. Najeeb
rules.relevance: This case holds that restrictions in Section 43D(5) do not oust the jurisdiction of a Constitutional Court to grant bail on grounds of violation of Part III of the Constitution, which is relevant to the Appellant's bail application.

rules.case_name: Angela Harish Sontakke v. State of Maharashtra
rules.reference: Angela Harish Sontakke v. State of Maharashtra
rules.relevance: This case relies on granting bail under UAPA despite Section 43-D(5) due to five years' incarceration and large number of witnesses, which is relevant to the Appellant's prolonged custody.

rules.reference: Uttar Pradesh Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972
rules.relevance: This provision allows a tenant to avoid eviction if they pay or tender the entire amount of rent and damages due at the first hearing of the suit, which is directly relevant to the respondent's claim of protection under this section.

rules.reference: Uttar Pradesh (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947
rules.relevance: Section 7-C allows a tenant to deposit rent in court if the landlord refuses to accept it or if there is a dispute regarding ownership, which is relevant to the respondent's lump sum deposits of rent.

rules.case_name: Brahmanand v. Kaushalya Devi
rules.reference: Brahmanand v. Kaushalya Devi
rules.relevance: Established that a mere deposit under Section 7-C is not a complete defense to eviction; the tenant must prove the circumstances justifying the deposit, such as the landlord's refusal to accept rent, which is relevant to the respondent's lump sum deposits.

rules.case_name: Kameshwar Singh Srivastava v. IV Addl. District Judge, Lucknow
rules.reference: Kameshwar Singh Srivastava v. IV Addl. District Judge, Lucknow
rules.relevance: Confirmed that while a valid deposit deems rent paid, courts in eviction proceedings must determine if the deposit was justified and not merely a harassment tactic, which is relevant to the respondent's lump sum deposits.

rules.reference: Uttar Pradesh Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972
rules.relevance: Establishes the ground for eviction if a tenant is in arrears of rent for not less than four months and fails to pay within one month of a demand notice, which is relevant to the appellant's claim of non-payment of rent.

rules.reference: Uttar Pradesh (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947
rules.relevance: This section provides the statutory ground for eviction on account of default in payment of rent, which is directly relevant to the appellant's claim of non-payment of rent.

rules.reference: Res Judicata
rules.relevance: An order permitting deposit under Section 7-C is a neutral, provisional act and does not operate as res judicata in subsequent eviction proceedings; the issue of whether the deposit was validly made can be re-agitated, which is relevant to the respondent's lump sum deposits.

rules.reference: Concurrent Findings of Fact
rules.relevance: Appellate courts generally do not interfere with concurrent findings of fact made by lower courts unless there is a perversity or legal error, which is relevant to the High Court's affirmation of the Trial Court's findings.

rules.reference: U.P. Urban Building (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972
rules.relevance: Permits a tenant to deposit rent in court if the landlord refuses to accept it, but explicitly states this right continues only 'until the landlord in the meantime signifies by notice in writing to the tenant his willingness to accept it,' which is relevant to the respondent's lump sum deposits.

rules.case_name: Gokaran Singh v. Ist Additional District and Sessions Judge, Hardoi and Ors.
rules.reference: Gokaran Singh v. Ist Additional District and Sessions Judge, Hardoi and Ors.
rules.relevance: Held that if a landlord serves a formal notice of demand expressing willingness to accept rent, the tenant is obligated to tender the admitted rent to the landlord and has no right to continue depositing it in court under Section 30(1), which is relevant to the respondent's lump sum deposits.

rules.reference: Maharashtra Control of Organised Crime Act, 1999
rules.relevance: This provision imposes a statutory bar on granting bail unless the court is satisfied that there are reasonable grounds for believing the accused is not guilty and is not likely to commit any offence while on bail. Relevant to the High Court's rejection of the appellant's bail application.

rules.case_name: Ranjitsing Brahmajeetsing Sharma v. State of Maharashtra and Anr.
rules.reference: Ranjitsing Brahmajeetsing Sharma v. State of Maharashtra and Anr.
rules.relevance: This precedent establishes that bail restrictions under MCOCA should not be pushed too far and that the 'probability test' applies. Relevant to assessing whether the High Court erred in applying the twin conditions for bail.

rules.case_name: Ranjitsing Brahmajeetsing Sharma vs. State of Maharashtra & Anr.
rules.reference: Ranjitsing Brahmajeetsing Sharma vs. State of Maharashtra & Anr.
rules.relevance: This precedent holds that under MCOCA, the court must probe deeper into materials to arrive at a finding that investigation materials may not justify a judgment of conviction. Relevant to evaluating the evidence presented by the appellant.

rules.reference: Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973
rules.relevance: This provision governs the entitlement to default bail if the charge sheet is not filed within 90 days. Relevant to the prolonged detention of the appellant without the framing of charges.

rules.case_name: Chaganti Satyanarayana and Others vs. State of Andhra Pradesh
rules.reference: Chaganti Satyanarayana and Others vs. State of Andhra Pradesh
rules.relevance: This precedent establishes that the 90-day period for filing a charge sheet under Section 167(2) Cr.P.C. begins from the date of the first order of remand by the Magistrate, not the date of arrest. Relevant to determining the appellant's entitlement to default bail.

rules.case_name: Sanjay Dutt vs. State
rules.reference: Sanjay Dutt vs. State
rules.relevance: This precedent holds that the right to default bail under Section 167(2) is lost once the charge sheet is filed, even if the application is pending. Relevant to the appellant's prolonged detention.

rules.reference: Constitution of India
rules.relevance: This provision protects personal liberty and must be balanced with public interest in serious crimes. Relevant to the appellant's argument that prolonged detention violates fundamental rights.

rules.case_name: Ram Govind Upadhyay v. Sudarshan Singh and Others
rules.reference: Ram Govind Upadhyay v. Sudarshan Singh and Others
rules.relevance: This precedent establishes that bail discretion must be exercised judiciously, considering the heinous nature of the crime, severity of punishment, and prima facie evidence. Relevant to evaluating the High Court's decision.

rules.case_name: Prasanta Kumar Sarkar v. Ashis Chatterjee and another
rules.reference: Prasanta Kumar Sarkar v. Ashis Chatterjee and another
rules.relevance: This precedent lists factors for bail consideration including prima facie grounds, gravity of accusation, danger of absconding, and character of the accused. Relevant to assessing the appellant's bail application.

rules.case_name: Prahlad Singh Bhati v. NCT, Delhi and Another
rules.reference: Prahlad Singh Bhati v. NCT, Delhi and Another
rules.relevance: This precedent cites factors to consider in bail, including nature of accusations, severity of punishment, and apprehension of witness tampering. Relevant to the appellant's argument regarding evidence and reasonable doubt.

rules.reference: Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002
rules.relevance: Defines the stringent conditions for bail under PMLA, which the Appellant must overcome to be granted bail.

rules.case_name: Vijay Madanlal Choudhary & Ors. v. Union of India & Ors.
rules.reference: Vijay Madanlal Choudhary & Ors. v. Union of India & Ors.
rules.relevance: Establishes that PMLA proceedings are contingent on a scheduled offence and are not extinguished unless the accused is finally absolved, which is relevant to the predicate offence issue.

rules.case_name: Enforcement Directorate vs. Preeti Chandra
rules.citation: Order dated 04.08.2023 in SLP (Crl.) No. 7409 of 2023
rules.reference: Enforcement Directorate vs. Preeti Chandra
rules.relevance: Confirms that the proviso to Section 45 of the PMLA confers discretion on the court to grant bail, which is relevant to the Appellant's bail application.

rules.case_name: Nikesh Tarachand Shah v. Union of India
rules.reference: Nikesh Tarachand Shah v. Union of India
rules.relevance: Struck down the twin conditions in Section 45 of PMLA as unconstitutional, which is relevant to the Appellant's argument regarding the conditions for bail.

rules.case_name: The Asst. Director Enforcement Directorate Vs. Dr. V.C. Mohan
rules.reference: The Asst. Director Enforcement Directorate Vs. Dr. V.C. Mohan
rules.relevance: Clarified that the rigour of Section 45 of the PMLA applies to anticipatory bail applications under Section 438 Cr.PC, which is relevant to the Appellant's bail arguments.

rules.case_name: Y.S. Jagan Mohan Reddy v. CBI
rules.reference: Y.S. Jagan Mohan Reddy v. CBI
rules.relevance: Held that economic offences constitute a class apart and need a different approach in the matter of bail, which is relevant to the Appellant's case involving a recruitment scam.

rules.case_name: P. Chidambaram Vs. Directorate of Enforcement
rules.reference: P. Chidambaram Vs. Directorate of Enforcement
rules.relevance: Established the principle that courts must be very slow in exercising discretion under Section 438 Cr.PC for serious economic offences, which is relevant to the Appellant's bail application.

rules.case_name: Prahlad Singh Bhati v. NCT, Delhi
rules.reference: Prahlad Singh Bhati v. NCT, Delhi
rules.relevance: Establishes factors for bail consideration, including the nature of the accusation and the character of the accused, which are relevant to the Appellant's bail application.

rules.case_name: State of U.P. through CBI v. Amarmani Tripathi
rules.reference: State of U.P. through CBI v. Amarmani Tripathi
rules.relevance: Holds that vague allegations of tampering are insufficient to refuse bail unless there is material showing the accused will use liberty to subvert justice, which is relevant to the Appellant's bail arguments.

rules.case_name: Hussainara Khatoon v. Home Secretary, State of Bihar
rules.reference: Hussainara Khatoon v. Home Secretary, State of Bihar
rules.relevance: Established that keeping undertrials behind bars without trial for long periods violates Article 21, which is relevant to the Appellant's argument regarding prolonged incarceration.

rules.case_name: Asha vs. Pt. B.D. Sharma UHS
rules.reference: Asha vs. Pt. B.D. Sharma UHS
rules.relevance: Supports the idea that in rare cases where no fault is attributable to the candidate and authorities are at fault, admission can be directed even after the cut-off date.

rules.case_name: Chandigarh Admn. vs. Jasmine Kaur
rules.reference: Chandigarh Admn. vs. Jasmine Kaur
rules.relevance: Overrules the view that compensation is the only relief available when the cut-off date has passed, holding instead that admission can be granted in exceptional circumstances.

rules.reference: Article 14 of the Constitution of India
rules.relevance: Denial of fair treatment and admission violates the right to equality and equal treatment under Article 14.

rules.reference: Article 21 of the Constitution of India
rules.relevance: Denial of admission jeopardizes the candidate's rights under Article 21.

rules.reference: Restitution is the norm, compensation is an exception
rules.relevance: In cases of violation of constitutional rights, the primary relief is restitutionary (restoring the status quo) and compensation is merely additional, not a substitute.

rules.reference: Article 226 and Article 32 of the Constitution of India
rules.relevance: Discusses the powers of High Courts and the Supreme Court to fashion appropriate remedies, including directing admission in exceptional cases.

rules.reference: Duty of candidate to verify eligibility criteria
rules.relevance: Every candidate is expected to thoroughly read advertisements and eligibility criteria, and must state correct particulars in the application form.

rules.reference: Judicial discipline and coordinate bench orders
rules.relevance: Courts must adhere to judicial discipline and not contradict established principles or coordinate bench orders.

rules.reference: Non-interference with Completed Academic Processes
rules.relevance: Courts generally do not interfere with admissions already effected and academic processes that have progressed significantly, to avoid injustice and disruption.

rules.reference: Equitable relief in absence of mala fide or prejudice
rules.relevance: Where admissions are merit-based, no higher-ranked candidate is prejudiced, and the admitting authority acted without mala fide intent, procedural irregularities should not lead to cancellation of admissions at a late stage.

rules.reference: Central Excise Tariff Act, 1985
rules.relevance: Directly addresses the classification of coconut oil as 'Edible oil' under Heading 1513, which is the primary contention of the respondents.

rules.reference: Central Excise Tariff Act, 1985
rules.relevance: Relevant to the Revenue's argument for classifying the coconut oil as 'Hair oil' under Heading 3305, which attracts a higher duty rate.

rules.reference: Central Excise Tariff Act, 1985
rules.relevance: Critical for interpreting whether the packaging and marketing of the coconut oil determine its classification under Chapter 33.

rules.provision: Rule 1 of General Rules for Interpretation
rules.reference: Central Excise Tariff Act, 1985
rules.relevance: Provides the foundational rule for determining classification based on headings and notes, which is central to resolving the dispute.

rules.provision: Rule 3 of General Rules for Interpretation
rules.reference: Central Excise Tariff Act, 1985
rules.relevance: Relevant for determining the hierarchy of classification rules, especially when multiple headings might apply.

rules.case_name: Collector of Central Excise, Shillong v. Wood Craft Products Ltd.
rules.reference: Collector of Central Excise, Shillong v. Wood Craft Products Ltd.
rules.relevance: Supports the use of HSN as a safe guide for resolving tariff classification disputes, which is pertinent to the alignment with HSN in the 2005 amendment.

rules.reference: Harmonised System of Nomenclature (HSN) as a safe guide
rules.relevance: Directly related to the alignment of the Central Excise Tariff with HSN post-2005 amendment, which affects the classification of coconut oil.

rules.reference: Common Parlance Test
rules.relevance: Relevant for determining whether the coconut oil is commonly understood as 'edible oil' or 'hair oil' based on its marketing and packaging.

rules.case_name: Camlin Limited v. Commissioner of Central Excise, Mumbai
rules.reference: Camlin Limited v. Commissioner of Central Excise, Mumbai
rules.relevance: Supports the dissenting view that HSN cannot override specific entries or notes in the Tariff Act, which is crucial for the Revenue's argument.

rules.reference: Principle against re-classification without change in product character

rules.case_name: All India Judges’ Association v. Union of India

rules.relevance: Established the quota system for recruitment to the Higher Judicial Service, which is foundational to the current debate on modifying the recruitment process.

rules.reference: Article 233 of the Constitution of India

rules.case_name: All India Judges Association v. Union of India

rules.reference: Gujarat State Judicial Service Rules, 2005

rules.reference: Doctrine of Proportionality

rules.case_name: Coimbatore District Central Coop. Bank v. Employees Assn.

rules.case_name: Bhagat Ram v. State of Himachal Pradesh

rules.relevance: Establishes that a penalty disproportionate to the gravity of misconduct violates Article 14, relevant to evaluating the punishment imposed.

rules.case_name: M.P. Gangadharan & Anr. v. State of Kerala & Ors.

rules.case_name: Capt. Harish Uppal v. Union of India & Ors.

rules.reference: Constitution of India

rules.reference: Irretrievable Breakdown of Marriage

rules.case_name: R. Srinivas Kumar v. R. Shametha

rules.relevance: Established that the Supreme Court can exercise powers under Article 142 to grant divorce on the ground of irretrievable breakdown in rare cases where the marriage is a dead letter, emotionally dead, and beyond salvage.

rules.case_name: Shilpa Sailesh v. Varun Sreenivasan
rules.reference: Shilpa Sailesh v. Varun Sreenivasan
rules.relevance: The Court relied on this precedent to establish the parameters and factors for granting divorce on the ground of irretrievable breakdown under Article 142(1), including the duration of separation, attempts at settlement, and welfare of children.

rules.case_name: Sukhendu Das v. Rita Mukherjee

rules.case_name: Union of India v. Saraswat Trading Agency and others

rules.case_name: Union of India v. Bright Power Projects (India) (P) Ltd.

rules.case_name: Garg Builders v. Bharat Heavy Electricals Limited

rules.relevance: Held that if a contract expressly bars payment of interest, the arbitrator cannot grant pendente lite interest, and clauses barring interest on 'any moneys due' are wide enough to cover arbitral awards.

rules.case_name: State of Rajasthan v. Ferro Concrete Construction Pvt. Ltd.

rules.case_name: Secretary, Irrigation Department, Government of Orissa v. G.C. Roy

rules.case_name: Hindustan Construction Co. Ltd. v. State of J & K

rules.case_name: Bhagawati Oxypen Ltd. v. Hindustan Copper Ltd.

rules.reference: Presumption of Innocence

rules.reference: Benefit of Doubt
rules.relevance: Where two views are possible, the one favorable to the accused must be upheld. The High Court's reliance on CDRs and presumption of presence may not meet this standard.

rules.reference: Chain of Circumstantial Evidence
rules.relevance: The prosecution must establish a complete chain of circumstantial evidence excluding all reasonable hypotheses of innocence. The High Court's reliance on CDRs and presence alone may not suffice.

rules.case_name: Dhanna v. State of MP
rules.reference: Dhanna v. State of MP
rules.relevance: Establishes the principles for reversing an acquittal, requiring the appellate court to justify its decision with strong evidence, which may be lacking here.

rules.case_name: Chandrappa v. State of Karnataka
rules.reference: Chandrappa v. State of Karnataka
rules.relevance: Requires a double presumption in favor of the accused in appellate proceedings involving acquittal, which the High Court may have overlooked.

rules.case_name: Kanhaiya Lal v. State of Rajasthan

rules.case_name: Sharad Birdhichand Sarda v. State of Maharashtra

rules.relevance: Lays down the five golden principles for conviction on circumstantial evidence, requiring a complete chain excluding innocence, which may not be met here.

rules.reference: Standard of Appellate Interference

rules.reference: Standard of Proof

rules.case_name: Babu v. State of Kerala

rules.relevance: Establishes that an appellate court should not interfere with an acquittal if two views are possible, unless the trial court's view is perverse, which may apply here.

rules.reference: Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996

rules.reference: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908

rules.reference: Functus Officio

rules.reference: Res Judicata
rules.relevance: Applies to prevent the re-agitation of issues already decided, which is relevant to the finality of the court's order appointing an arbitrator and disposing of the Section 11(6) petition.

rules.case_name: Satyadhvan Ghosal v. Deorajin Debi
rules.reference: Satyadhvan Ghosal v. Deorajin Debi
rules.relevance: Established that res judicata applies between stages of the same litigation to prevent re-agitation of matters already decided, which is relevant to the finality of the court's order.

rules.case_name: Hope Plantations Ltd. v. Taluk Land Board, Peermade
rules.reference: Hope Plantations Ltd. v. Taluk Land Board, Peermade
rules.relevance: Supported the public policy basis of res judicata, emphasizing finality of decisions and preventing double litigation, which is relevant to the court's jurisdiction post-appointment.

rules.case_name: SBP & Co. v. Patel Engineering Ltd. and Anr.
rules.reference: SBP & Co. v. Patel Engineering Ltd. and Anr.
rules.relevance: Established that the power under Section 11(6) is judicial, requires a reasoned order, and mandates hearing both parties on preliminary aspects, which is relevant to the court's jurisdiction.

rules.reference: Judicial nature of Section 11(6) power
rules.relevance: The Chief Justice must exercise judicial discretion, requiring verification of facts, consideration of objections, and a reasoned order, which is relevant to the court's jurisdiction post-appointment.

rules.reference: Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996
rules.relevance: The court considered the maintainability of the application for appointment of an arbitrator under this section, which is relevant to the jurisdiction of the court.

rules.reference: Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996
rules.relevance: Establishes the doctrine of separability, mandating that an arbitration clause be treated as an agreement independent of the other terms of the contract, remaining enforceable even if the contract is null and void, which is relevant to the jurisdiction of the court.

rules.reference: Constitution of India
rules.relevance: Relevant to the issue of whether the distinction between work-charged employees and job contractors under the Odisha Pension Rules violates the principle of equality under Article 14 of the Constitution.

rules.case_name: D.S. Nakara v. Union of India
rules.reference: D.S. Nakara v. Union of India
rules.relevance: Relevant to the interpretation of pension rules and the principle that distinctions in pension benefits must have a rational nexus to the object of the policy and cannot be arbitrary.

rules.case_name: Indian Ex-Services League v. Union of India
rules.reference: Indian Ex-Services League v. Union of India
rules.relevance: Relevant to the principle that Nakara does not mandate identical amounts of pension for all retirees irrespective of date of retirement if reckonable emoluments differ.

rules.case_name: D.S. Nakara & Ors. v. Union of India & Ors.

rules.case_name: Krishena Kumar v. Union of India
rules.reference: Krishena Kumar v. Union of India
rules.relevance: Relevant to the principle that specifying a date for new regulations is valid if not arbitrary or discriminatory.

rules.case_name: Union of India v. P.N. Menon

rules.relevance: Relevant to the principle that fixing a cut-off date for merging dearness allowance with pay is not arbitrary if based on reasonable considerations like price index levels.

rules.case_name: S.C. Chandra v. State of Jharkhand
rules.reference: S.C. Chandra v. State of Jharkhand
rules.relevance: Relevant to the principle that the doctrine of 'equal pay for equal work' applies only when there is total identity between two groups of employees.

rules.case_name: Union of India v. All India Services Pensioners' Association and Another
rules.reference: Union of India v. All India Services Pensioners' Association and Another
rules.relevance: Relevant to the principle that the principles in Nakara cannot be extended to gratuity payments and that emoluments of retirees before and after a notified date need not be treated as the same.

rules.case_name: K.L. Rathee v. Union of India
rules.reference: K.L. Rathee v. Union of India
rules.relevance: Relevant to the principle that Nakara did not strike down the definition of emoluments and that pension calculation must be based on emoluments drawn at the time of retirement.

rules.case_name: Barauni Refinery Pragatisheel Shramik Parishad v. Indian Oil Corporation Ltd.
rules.reference: Barauni Refinery Pragatisheel Shramik Parishad v. Indian Oil Corporation Ltd.
rules.relevance: Relevant to the principle that settlements reached in conciliation carry a presumption of being just and fair; the burden is on the challenger to prove otherwise.

rules.reference: Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973

rules.case_name: State of Haryana & Ors. v. Bhajan Lal & Ors.

rules.relevance: This precedent establishes the categories of cases where quashing of FIRs is justified, including when allegations do not prima facie constitute an offence or are mala fide.

rules.reference: Indian Penal Code

rules.reference: Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973

rules.case_name: Iqbal Singh Marwah v. Meenakshi Marwah

rules.reference: Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973

rules.reference: Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973
rules.relevance: This provision empowers the Magistrate to discharge the accused if no sufficient ground for proceeding exists, which is relevant to the appellant's argument that the proceedings should be quashed.

rules.case_name: State of Haryana and Ors. v. Bhajan Lal and Ors.

rules.case_name: State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal

rules.relevance: This precedent confirms that socio-economic amelioration under the Act extinguishes pre-existing limited estates and confers absolute ownership if there is a pre-existing vestige of title, which is relevant to Geeta Sharma's claim.

rules.reference: Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956
rules.relevance: This section provides the statutory basis for a wife's claim to maintenance, which is relevant to Geeta Sharma's claim.

rules.case_name: Thankam v. Rajan
rules.reference: Thankam v. Rajan
rules.relevance: This precedent supports the view that remarriage of a wife is not a ground for losing the right to succeed to her deceased husband's property, which is relevant to Geeta Sharma's claim.

rules.reference: Hindu Succession Act, 1956
rules.relevance: This section establishes that any property possessed by a female Hindu shall be held by her as a full owner, not as a limited owner, if acquired in recognition of a pre-existing right, which is relevant to Geeta Sharma's claim.

rules.reference: Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881
rules.relevance: Establishes vicarious liability for persons in charge of and responsible for the conduct of the business of the company at the time the offence was committed.

rules.case_name: SMS Pharmaceuticals Ltd. v. Neeta Bhalla
rules.reference: SMS Pharmaceuticals Ltd. v. Neeta Bhalla
rules.relevance: Held that specific averments are required in the complaint to make a director liable under Section 141, and there is no deemed liability for directors merely by virtue of their position.

rules.case_name: K.K. Ahuja v. V.K. Arora
rules.reference: K.K. Ahuja v. V.K. Arora
rules.relevance: Summarized that for a Director (who is not a Managing Director or signatory), an averment that they were in charge of and responsible for the business is necessary, and no further averment is strictly necessary though particulars are desirable.

rules.case_name: Sabitha Ramamurthy v. R.B.S. Channabasavaradhya
rules.reference: Sabitha Ramamurthy v. R.B.S. Channabasavaradhya
rules.relevance: Reiterated that strict compliance with statutory requirements is necessary to infer vicarious liability under Section 141.

rules.case_name: Gunwala Sales Pvt. Ltd. v. Anu Mehta
rules.reference: Gunwala Sales Pvt. Ltd. v. Anu Mehta
rules.relevance: Held that basic averments are sufficient to send a Director to trial unless incontrovertible evidence is produced to show they were not in charge of the business.

rules.case_name: N.K. Wahi vs. Shekhar Singh & Ors.
rules.reference: N.K. Wahi vs. Shekhar Singh & Ors.
rules.relevance: Reiterated that without clear averments regarding the role of directors, prosecution cannot be maintained.

rules.case_name: S.M.S. Pharmaceuticals Ltd. vs. Neeta Bhalla & Anr.
rules.reference: S.M.S. Pharmaceuticals Ltd. vs. Neeta Bhalla & Anr.
rules.relevance: Held that specific averments in the complaint are essential to satisfy Section 141, stating that the accused must be alleged to be in charge of and responsible for the business at the time of the offence; mere directorship is not sufficient.

rules.case_name: Kalla Sujatha v. Fertilizers & Chemicals Travancore Ltd.
rules.reference: Kalla Sujatha v. Fertilizers & Chemicals Travancore Ltd.
rules.relevance: Held that liability cannot be fastened if it is not stated that the accused was in charge of the business and responsible for its conduct.

rules.case_name: Aneeta Hada v. Godmother Travels and Tours Private Limited
rules.reference: Aneeta Hada v. Godmother Travels and Tours Private Limited
rules.relevance: Held that vicarious liability under Section 141 cannot exist unless the company itself is prosecuted.

rules.case_name: Ashutosh Ashok Parasrampuria v. Gharrkul Industries Pvt. Ltd.
rules.reference: Ashutosh Ashok Parasrampuria v. Gharrkul Industries Pvt. Ltd.
rules.relevance: Held that High Courts should not quash complaints unless unimpeachable evidence shows the director could not have been concerned with the issuance of cheques.

rules.reference: Constitution of India
rules.relevance: The exclusion of persons appointed on an academic arrangement for a fixed term from regularization under Section 3(b) of the 2010 Act raises questions of equality and non-arbitrary state action.

rules.reference: Constitution of India
rules.relevance: The right to equal opportunity in public employment is relevant to the appellants' claim for regularization despite the exclusion in Section 3(b).

rules.reference: Constitution of India
rules.relevance: The mandatory role of the Public Service Commission in recruitment is relevant to the validity of the appellants' appointments and the exclusion under Section 3(b).

rules.case_name: State of Karnataka vs. Umadevi
rules.reference: State of Karnataka vs. Umadevi
rules.relevance: This Constitution Bench decision establishes that regularization is not a source of recruitment and that courts should not issue directions for regularization of illegal appointments.

rules.case_name: State of Rajasthan vs. Daya Lal
rules.reference: State of Rajasthan vs. Daya Lal
rules.relevance: Established that a High Court cannot regularize an employee in exercise of its power under Article 226, which is relevant to the High Court's dismissal of the appellants' petitions.

rules.case_name: State of U.P. vs. Kaushal Kishore Shukla
rules.reference: State of U.P. vs. Kaushal Kishore Shukla
rules.relevance: Established the principle that a temporary employee has no right to the post, which is relevant to the appellants' claim for regularization.

rules.case_name: Keshav Chandra Joshi v. Union of India
rules.reference: Keshav Chandra Joshi v. Union of India
rules.relevance: Establishes the distinction between 'rules of recruitment' and 'conditions of service', holding that recruitment rules cannot be relaxed, which is relevant to the exclusion under Section 3(b).

rules.reference: Regularisation cannot bypass prescribed selection procedure
rules.relevance: The principle that long service on an ad-hoc basis does not entitle an employee to regularization if the mandatory selection process prescribed by the employer's rules has not been followed is relevant to the appellants' claim.

rules.reference: Statutory Recruitment Rules
rules.relevance: The principle that regular appointment requires selection by the Public Service Commission is relevant to the validity of the appellants' appointments and the exclusion under Section 3(b).

rules.case_name: Dr. M.A. Haque & Ors. v. Union of India & Ors.
rules.reference: Dr. M.A. Haque & Ors. v. Union of India & Ors.
rules.relevance: Deprecates the practice of bypassing the Public Service Commission or prescribed selection procedures, which opens a back door for illegal recruitment, relevant to the appellants' claim.

rules.reference: Electricity Act, 2003
rules.relevance: Vests the Appropriate Commission with the power to determine tariffs for supply, transmission, and retail sale, which is directly relevant to the CERC's jurisdiction in levying compensatory charges.

rules.reference: Electricity Act, 2003
rules.relevance: Lays down principles for tariff determination, including commercial principles and safeguarding consumer interests, which may inform the CERC's decision-making process.

rules.case_name: Transmission Corporation of Andhra Pradesh Vs. Sai Renewable Power Pvt. Ltd.
rules.reference: Transmission Corporation of Andhra Pradesh Vs. Sai Renewable Power Pvt. Ltd.
rules.relevance: Established that tariff fixation is a statutory function of the Regulatory Commission, not merely a contractual agreement, supporting the CERC's authority to levy compensatory charges.

rules.case_name: Energy Watchdog v. Central Electricity Regulatory Commission
rules.reference: Energy Watchdog v. Central Electricity Regulatory Commission
rules.relevance: Established that changes in Indian law, including statutory documents like the Tariff Policy and NCDP, constitute 'Change in Law' and trigger restitutionary compensation, which may be relevant to the CERC's compensatory charges.

rules.reference: Electricity Act, 2003
rules.relevance: Defines the right to appeal to the Appellate Tribunal for 'any person aggrieved' by an order of the Appropriate Commission, which is relevant to the maintainability of the writ petitions.

rules.reference: Non-interference with Concurrent Findings of Fact
rules.relevance: The Court should not interfere with concurrent findings of fact by expert regulatory bodies (CERC/SERC and APTEL) unless they are perverse, arbitrary, or contrary to law, which may be relevant to the High Court's intervention.

rules.case_name: Uttar Haryana Bijli Vitran Nigam Limited v. Adani Power Limited
rules.reference: Uttar Haryana Bijli Vitran Nigam Limited v. Adani Power Limited
rules.relevance: Interpreted Article 13.2 of the PPA, confirming the in-built restitutionary principle and the mechanism for claiming Change in Law compensation, which may be relevant to the compensatory charges.

rules.case_name: Uttar Haryana Bijli Vitran Nigam Limited v. Adani Power (Mundra) Limited
rules.reference: Uttar Haryana Bijli Vitran Nigam Limited v. Adani Power (Mundra) Limited
rules.relevance: Held that carrying cost must be calculated with compound interest from the date of the Change in Law event to effectuate restitution, which may be relevant to the compensatory charges.

rules.case_name: Maharashtra State Electricity Distribution Company Limited v. Maharashtra Electricity Regulatory Commission
rules.reference: Maharashtra State Electricity Distribution Company Limited v. Maharashtra Electricity Regulatory Commission
rules.relevance: Reinforced that courts cannot rewrite contracts and that explicit terms regarding LPS are binding, which may be relevant to the CERC's decision.

rules.case_name: Gujarat Urja Vikas Nigam Ltd. v. Essar Power Ltd.
rules.reference: Gujarat Urja Vikas Nigam Ltd. v. Essar Power Ltd.
rules.relevance: Established that Section 86(1)(f) gives the State Commission discretion to adjudicate or refer to arbitration, and that the special law overrides the general Arbitration Act, which may be relevant to the jurisdiction of the CERC.

rules.case_name: Dollar Co. v. Collector of Madras
rules.reference: Dollar Co. v. Collector of Madras
rules.relevance: Establishes that the sale price of the acquired land is the best evidence for determining its fair market value, which is directly relevant to the Reference Court's failure to consider the highest sale exemplar.

rules.case_name: Viluben Jhalejar Contractor (dead) By LRs. v. State of Gujarat
rules.reference: Viluben Jhalejar Contractor (dead) By LRs. v. State of Gujarat
rules.relevance: Established that courts must consider positive factors (e.g., proximity to roads, smallness of size) and negative factors (e.g., largeness of area, remoteness) when determining market value, which is relevant to the Reference Court's valuation method.

rules.case_name: Bhagwathula Samanna & Ors. v. Special Tehsildar
rules.reference: Bhagwathula Samanna & Ors. v. Special Tehsildar
rules.relevance: Held that deduction for small plot exemplars is not mandatory if the land is already developed or has high potential value, which is relevant to the Reference Court's application of a 20% deduction.

rules.case_name: Ashrafi & Ors. v. State of Haryana & Ors.
rules.reference: Ashrafi & Ors. v. State of Haryana & Ors.
rules.relevance: Emphasizes the belting system and requires that exemplar land must be similar to the acquired land, which is relevant to the Reference Court's selection of exemplars.

rules.case_name: Land Acquisition Officer, Kammarapally Village v. Nookala Rajamallu and Ors.
rules.reference: Land Acquisition Officer, Kammarapally Village v. Nookala Rajamallu and Ors.
rules.relevance: Establishes that while small plot rates are not a safe criterion for large acquisitions, they can be used with necessary deductions if no other material is available, which is relevant to the Reference Court's valuation approach.

rules.case_name: Smt. Basavva and Ors. v. Special Land Acquisition Officer and Ors.
rules.reference: Smt. Basavva and Ors. v. Special Land Acquisition Officer and Ors.
rules.relevance: Requires sufficient deductions to arrive at just market value when using small plot sales for large land acquisitions, considering factors like waiting periods, which is relevant to the Reference Court's deduction method.

rules.case_name: A.P. Industrial Infrastructure Corporation Limited v. G. Mohan Reddy & Ors.
rules.reference: A.P. Industrial Infrastructure Corporation Limited v. G. Mohan Reddy & Ors.
rules.relevance: Establishes that the situation of the land, particularly its distance from the National Highway, plays a vital role in fixing market value, which is relevant to the Reference Court's valuation of the land near Jintur town.

rules.reference: Comparable Sales Principle
rules.relevance: Comparable sales must be close in time to the Section 4 notification and similar in nature (size, location, access) to the acquired land, which is relevant to the Reference Court's selection and averaging of exemplars.

rules.reference: Appellate Interference
rules.relevance: An appellate court cannot arbitrarily enhance market value without cogent reasons when the lower court's valuation is supported by reliable contemporaneous sale deeds, which is relevant to the High Court's dismissal of the appeal.

rules.reference: Appreciation of evidence
rules.relevance: An appellate court must properly appreciate witness testimony and documentary evidence, including the implications of a party's failure to produce available records, which is relevant to the High Court's error in stating that the highest exemplar was considered.

rules.reference: Customs Act, 1962
rules.relevance: Relevant to the appellant's request for amendment of the shipping bills due to clerical error by the customs broker.

rules.case_name: Director General of Foreign Trade & Anr. v. Kanak Exports & Anr.
rules.reference: Director General of Foreign Trade & Anr. v. Kanak Exports & Anr.
rules.relevance: Establishes that incentive schemes are privileges that the Government can amend, modify, or rescind as policy decisions, and courts should not tinker with such economic policy decisions.

rules.reference: Principles of Natural Justice
rules.relevance: Relevant to the PRC's rejection of the appellant's claim without assigning reasons or affording an opportunity of hearing.

rules.reference: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992
rules.relevance: Empowers the Central Government to formulate, announce, and amend the Foreign Trade Policy, which is relevant to the MEIS scheme under which the appellant sought incentives.

rules.case_name: Union of India & Anr. vs. IndusInd Bank Limited & Anr.
rules.reference: Union of India & Anr. vs. IndusInd Bank Limited & Anr.
rules.relevance: Established that remedial amendments affecting accrued rights are prospective, not retrospective, which may be relevant to the amendment allowed by the Deputy Commissioner of Customs.

rules.reference: Customs Act, 1962
rules.relevance: Establishes that the rate of duty for goods entered for home consumption is the rate in force on the date the bill of entry is presented, which may be relevant to the timing of the amendment.

rules.case_name: Bharat Surfactants (Pvt.) Ltd. v. Union of India
rules.reference: Bharat Surfactants (Pvt.) Ltd. v. Union of India
rules.relevance: Held that the date of presentation of the Bill of Entry is the relevant date for determining the rate of duty, which may be relevant to the timing of the amendment.

rules.reference: Substantial compliance with statutory conditions
rules.relevance: Relevant to whether the appellant's claim should be considered despite the clerical error, as the error was corrected by the Deputy Commissioner of Customs.

rules.reference: Customs Act, 1962
rules.relevance: Mandates the deposit of penalty pending appeal, with a proviso allowing the Tribunal to dispense with such deposit if it causes 'undue hardship', which may be relevant to the appellant's appeal.

rules.case_name: S. Vasudeva v. State of Karnataka and Ors.
rules.reference: S. Vasudeva v. State of Karnataka and Ors.
rules.relevance: Defined 'undue hardship' as economic hardship that is not merited by the conduct of the claimant or is disproportionate to the circumstances, which may be relevant to the appellant's appeal.

rules.reference: Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973
rules.relevance: This section mandates previous sanction for prosecuting public servants for offences committed while acting or purporting to act in the discharge of official duty. The appellants' actions as public servants in certifying mutation entries may fall under this protection if they were acting in their official capacity.

rules.case_name: Shambhu Nath Misra v. State of U.P.
rules.reference: Shambhu Nath Misra v. State of U.P.
rules.relevance: Held that fabrication of records or misappropriation of funds is not an official duty, even if the official position enabled the act, and thus does not attract Section 197 protection. This precedent is relevant to determine if the appellants' actions were within their official duties or amounted to misconduct.

rules.reference: Inordinate and Unexplained Delay
rules.relevance: A significant, unexplained delay in lodging an FIR, especially when the complainant was aware of the dispute earlier, raises doubts about the bona fides of the complaint. The 20-year delay in this case may affect the credibility of the prosecution's case.

rules.case_name: State of Haryana & Ors. v. Bhajan Lal & Ors.
rules.reference: State of Haryana & Ors. v. Bhajan Lal & Ors.
rules.relevance: Holds that the power to quash criminal prosecution should be exercised very sparingly and with circumspection, particularly regarding allegations of malafide, and only in the rarest of rare cases. This precedent is relevant to assess whether the FIR was lodged with mala fide intentions.

rules.reference: Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973
rules.relevance: Confers inherent powers on the High Court to secure the ends of justice and prevent abuse of the process of law. This section is relevant to determine if the High Court can quash the FIR based on the unexplained delay and other factors.

rules.case_name: Siddharam Satlingappa Mhetre v. State of Maharashtra
rules.reference: Siddharam Satlingappa Mhetre v. State of Maharashtra
rules.relevance: Laid down parameters for granting anticipatory bail, including nature of accusation, role of accused, and possibility of fleeing. This precedent is relevant to assess the High Court's decision to dismiss the anticipatory bail applications.

rules.reference: Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973
rules.relevance: The court considered the statutory ingredients and factors required for granting anticipatory bail, noting that the court must apply its mind to the stage of investigation and conduct of the accused. This section is relevant to the appellants' anticipatory bail applications.

rules.case_name: Sushila Aggarwal v. State (NCT of Delhi)
rules.reference: Sushila Aggarwal v. State (NCT of Delhi)
rules.relevance: Laid down principles for granting anticipatory bail, including consideration of the nature and gravity of the offence and the role of the accused. This precedent is relevant to the appellants' anticipatory bail applications.

rules.reference: Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973
rules.relevance: Empowers a Magistrate to order investigation by police into a cognizable offence before taking cognizance. This section is relevant to the investigation process in this case.

rules.case_name: Dablu Kujur v. State of Jharkhand
rules.reference: Dablu Kujur v. State of Jharkhand
rules.relevance: Crystallized the legal position that chargesheets must contain sufficient details and evidence to enable the Magistrate to take cognizance, not just a reproduction of the FIR. This precedent is relevant to assess the sufficiency of the prosecution's evidence.

rules.reference: Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988
rules.relevance: Primary charge against the accused for acquiring disproportionate assets.

rules.reference: Indian Penal Code, 1860
rules.relevance: Charge of abetment of the offence under the Prevention of Corruption Act.

rules.case_name: State of Tamil Nadu v. N. Suresh Rajan
rules.reference: State of Tamil Nadu v. N. Suresh Rajan
rules.relevance: Relied upon to hold that income tax assessments do not conclusively prove lawful sources of assets.

rules.case_name: P. Nallammal v. State
rules.reference: P. Nallammal v. State
rules.relevance: Relied upon to establish that private individuals can be prosecuted for abetting a public servant.

rules.case_name: K. Veeraswami v. Union of India
rules.reference: K. Veeraswami v. Union of India
rules.relevance: Relied upon to establish the burden on the accused to satisfactorily account for disproportionate assets.

rules.case_name: State of M.P. v. Awadh Kishore Gupta
rules.reference: State of M.P. v. Awadh Kishore Gupta
rules.relevance: Relied upon to define 'income' and 'known sources of income', clarifying that windfalls or gains from graft/crime do not constitute known sources of income for a public servant.

rules.reference: Criminal Law Amendment Ordinance, 1944
rules.relevance: Relevant for the attachment and forfeiture of property procured by means of offences under the Prevention of Corruption Act.

rules.reference: Benami Transactions
rules.relevance: The court applied principles of benami transactions to attribute assets held in the names of companies and associates to the public servant.

rules.reference: Indian Evidence Act, 1872
rules.relevance: The court applied this section to establish that facts specially within the knowledge of the accused, such as the source of unexplained wealth, are for the accused to explain.

rules.case_name: State of Karnataka v. Selvi J. Jayalalitha & Ors.
rules.reference: State of Karnataka v. Selvi J. Jayalalitha & Ors.
rules.relevance: Held that income tax returns and assessment orders are not conclusive proof of lawful sources of income for the purpose of Section 13(1)(e) of the PC Act.

rules.case_name: Union of India and Ors. v. Rajiv Yadav and Ors.
rules.reference: Union of India and Ors. v. Rajiv Yadav and Ors.
rules.relevance: Establishes that a selected candidate has no right to be allocated to a specific cadre or home state, as allocation is an incidence of service. Relevant to the appellant's claim for a specific cadre allocation.

rules.case_name: State of Haryana v. Subhash Chander Marwaha and Others
rules.reference: State of Haryana v. Subhash Chander Marwaha and Others
rules.relevance: Holds that the existence of vacancies does not confer a legal right on a selected candidate to be appointed. Supports the Union's argument that the vacancy was consumed when offered to Rishikesh Meena.

rules.case_name: Jitendra Kumar and Others v. State of Punjab and Others
rules.reference: Jitendra Kumar and Others v. State of Punjab and Others
rules.relevance: Held that candidates do not acquire any right merely by applying for selection or even after selection. Relevant to the appellant's claim based on non-joining of senior candidates.

rules.reference: Indian Police Service (Appointment by competitive Examination) Regulations, 1965
rules.relevance: Explicitly states that a candidate does not acquire a right to appointment by mere inclusion of his name in the merit list. Supports the Union's position on the appellant's claim.

rules.reference: No indefeasible right to appointment
rules.relevance: Notification of vacancies is an invitation to apply; selection does not create a right to appointment unless recruitment rules explicitly provide otherwise. Relevant to the appellant's claim for the vacancy.

rules.reference: Cadre allocation is an incidence of service
rules.relevance: Established that a selected candidate has no right to claim allocation to a specific cadre or home State. Members of All India Services bear liability to serve in any part of India, and allocation is a post-recruitment administrative decision. Relevant to the appellant's claim for a specific cadre allocation.

rules.case_name: M.V. Thimmaiah and others v. Union Public Service Commission and others
rules.reference: M.V. Thimmaiah and others v. Union Public Service Commission and others
rules.relevance: Holds that courts cannot sit as appellate authorities to examine Selection Committee recommendations unless there is mala fides or serious violation of statutory rules. Relevant to the appellant's challenge to the Ministry's handling of the vacancy.

rules.reference: Delay and Laches
rules.relevance: A belated challenge to cadre allocation, after officers have joined and undergone training, is not conducive to public interest and bars relief. Relevant to the appellant's claim after more than two decades.

rules.case_name: Union Public Service Commission v. M. Sathiya Priya and others
rules.reference: Union Public Service Commission v. M. Sathiya Priya and others
rules.relevance: Reinforces that courts have very limited scope of judicial review in matters of assessment by expert Selection Committees. Relevant to the appellant's challenge to the Ministry's decision.

rules.reference: IPS (Cadre) Rules, 1954
rules.relevance: Confers power on the Central Government to allocate IPS officers to various cadres in consultation with State Governments. Relevant to the Ministry's authority in handling the vacancy.

rules.reference: Constitution of India
rules.relevance: Protects the right to life and personal liberty, which includes protection against custodial torture and the right to live with human dignity.

rules.case_name: D. K. Basu v. State of West Bengal
rules.reference: D. K. Basu v. State of West Bengal
rules.relevance: Establishes safeguards against custodial violence and the State's responsibility for injuries sustained in custody, directly relevant to the appellant's allegations of torture.

rules.case_name: Nilabati Behera v. State of Orissa
rules.reference: Nilabati Behera v. State of Orissa
rules.relevance: Established that compensation is a public law remedy for contravention of fundamental rights, which may be applicable if the appellant's rights under Article 21 were violated.

rules.reference: Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973
rules.relevance: Mandates the registration of an FIR for cognizable offences, which is crucial for the appellant's claim that the police failed to register an FIR against the torturers.

rules.reference: Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973
rules.relevance: Governs the inquiry into death or grievous injuries, which is relevant to the appellant's medical condition and the failure to conduct a proper inquiry.

rules.case_name: State of West Bengal & others v. Committee for Protection of Democratic Rights, West Bengal and others
rules.reference: State of West Bengal & others v. Committee for Protection of Democratic Rights, West Bengal and others
rules.relevance: Established that Constitutional Courts can direct CBI investigation in exceptional situations to ensure a fair investigation, which is relevant to the appellant's request for CBI intervention.

rules.case_name: K. V. Rajendran v. Superintendent of Police, CBCID South Zone, Chennai and others
rules.reference: K. V. Rajendran v. Superintendent of Police, CBCID South Zone, Chennai and others
rules.relevance: Held that transfer to CBI is permissible in rare and exceptional cases where state police investigation lacks credibility, which may apply here due to the conflict of interest.

rules.reference: Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973
rules.relevance: Confers inherent powers on the High Court to quash an FIR if it is mala fide, which is relevant to the appellant's request to quash the FIR against him under Section 309 IPC.

rules.case_name: Himanshu Kumar and Ors. Vs. State of Chhattisgarh and Ors.
rules.reference: Himanshu Kumar and Ors. Vs. State of Chhattisgarh and Ors.
rules.relevance: Establishes that transfer of investigation to CBI is an extraordinary power to be exercised sparingly, which is relevant to the High Court's decision not to order a CBI investigation.

rules.case_name: Sheela Barse v. State of Maharashtra
rules.reference: Sheela Barse v. State of Maharashtra
rules.relevance: Directs Magistrates to inform arrested persons of their right to medical examination under Section 54 CrPC, which is relevant to the appellant's claim of denial of medical rights.

rules.reference: Constitution of India
rules.relevance: Protects laws relating to agrarian reforms from challenges under Articles 14, 19, and 31. The court held that the 1961 Act and its amendments, having received Presidential assent, are protected agrarian reforms.

rules.reference: Constitution of India
rules.relevance: Guarantees that no person shall be deprived of property save by authority of law. The court held that since the vesting was part of protected agrarian reforms, there was no violation of Article 300A.

rules.case_name: Ranjit Singh v. State of Punjab
rules.reference: Ranjit Singh v. State of Punjab
rules.relevance: Held that land reserved for common purposes by pro-rata cut vests in the Panchayat as part of agrarian reforms, and no compensation is payable. This applies to land outside ceiling limits.

rules.case_name: Ajit Singh v. State of Punjab
rules.reference: Ajit Singh v. State of Punjab
rules.relevance: Held that for land within ceiling limits, only management and control vest in the Panchayat, not title. This does not constitute 'acquisition by the State' requiring compensation under the second proviso to Article 31-A.

rules.case_name: Mahant Sankarshan Ramanuja Das Goswami v. State of Orissa
rules.reference: Mahant Sankarshan Ramanuja Das Goswami v. State of Orissa
rules.relevance: Held that an amending act receives the protection of Article 31-A if it is assented to by the President, as it extends the operation of the original law.

rules.case_name: Rajender Parshad & Ors. v. State of Haryana & Ors.
rules.reference: Rajender Parshad & Ors. v. State of Haryana & Ors.
rules.relevance: Struck down the Haryana Municipal Common Lands (Regulation) Act, 1974, as unconstitutional because it was not a measure of agrarian reform. The court applied this to the amendments to the Municipal Acts.

rules.reference: East Punjab Holdings (Consolidation and Prevention of Fragmentation) Act, 1948
rules.relevance: Empowered Consolidation Officers to assign land for common purposes and vested management of such lands in the Panchayat or State, forming the statutory basis for the deprivation of property.

rules.reference: East Punjab Holdings (Consolidation and Prevention of Fragmentation) Act, 1948
rules.relevance: Defined 'common purpose' broadly to include village welfare and validated previous rules, which the appellants challenged.

rules.case_name: Attar Singh v. The State of U.P.
rules.reference: Attar Singh v. The State of U.P.
rules.relevance: Sikri J. relied on this case to support the view that reservation of small bits of land for common purposes benefits the proprietors and does not amount to acquisition by the State requiring compensation.

rules.reference: Punjab Village Common Lands (Regulation) Act, 1961
rules.relevance: Defines 'shamilat deh' to include lands described in revenue records as 'shamilat deh' or 'charand', establishing that charand land vests in the Gram Panchayat.

rules.reference: Consumer Protection Act, 1986
rules.relevance: Defines 'consumer' and excludes persons who obtain goods or services for a 'commercial purpose'. The court interpreted this exclusion to determine the Appellant's status.

rules.case_name: Laxmi Engineering Works v. P.S.G. Industrial Institute
rules.reference: Laxmi Engineering Works v. P.S.G. Industrial Institute
rules.relevance: Established that 'commercial purpose' requires a close nexus with profit-generating activity and that the Explanation clause is clarificatory, not exhaustive.

rules.case_name: Paramount Digital Colour Lab v. Agfa India Private Limited
rules.reference: Paramount Digital Colour Lab v. Agfa India Private Limited
rules.relevance: Re-emphasized the requirement of a 'close nexus' between the purchase and large-scale profit activity to classify a transaction as commercial.

rules.case_name: Spring Meadows Hospital v. Harjol Ahluwalia
rules.reference: Spring Meadows Hospital v. Harjol Ahluwalia
rules.relevance: Supported the principle that a person hiring services for a beneficiary (such as an employer for employees) can be included in the definition of 'consumer'.

rules.reference: Dominant Purpose Test
rules.relevance: The court applied this test to determine that the dominant purpose of buying flats was employee welfare, not profit generation.

rules.reference: Close Nexus Test
